questions.question: Let $V_1$ and $V_2$ be convex sets in $\mathbb{R}^n$. Which of the following sets is convex for every such pair $V_1$, $V_2$?
For convex sets $V_1,V_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ and fixed real numbers $\alpha_1,\alpha_2$, which set is denoted by $\alpha_1V_1+\alpha_2V_2$?
Let $V_1,V_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be convex. For which real coefficients $\alpha_1,\alpha_2$ is the set $\alpha_1V_1+\alpha_2V_2$ guaranteed to be convex?
Let $\{V_i\colon i\in I\}$ be an infinite collection of convex sets in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $W=\bigcap_{i\in I}V_i$. What can be said about the convexity of $W$?
options: $W$ need not be convex, since only finite intersections keep convexity.
$W$ is convex for every such collection of convex sets.
$W$ is convex if nonempty; an empty $W$ does not count as convex.
$W$ is convex only when every $V_i$ is also closed.

questions.question: A linear program has feasible region $F=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon \boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\le b_i\text{ for }i=1,\dots,m\}$ with every $\boldsymbol{a}_i\neq\boldsymbol{0}$ and objective $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$. Why is $F$ convex?
options: The objective $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ is linear, which makes $F$ convex.
$F$ is closed, and closed sets given by weak inequalities are convex.
$F$ is an intersection of halfspaces, each of which is convex.
$F$ is a sum of halfspaces, and sums of convex sets are convex.

questions.question: Two segments in $\mathbb{R}^2$ are given: $V_1=\{(t,t)\colon 0\le t\le1\}$ and $V_2=\{(s,0)\colon 0\le s\le2\}$. What shape is their sum $V_1+V_2$?
options: The line segment joining the points $(0,0)$ and $(3,1)$

questions.question: For the intervals $V_1=[0,1]$ and $V_2=[1,2]$ in $\mathbb{R}$, compute the linear combination $2V_1-3V_2=\{2x_1-3x_2\colon x_1\in V_1,\ x_2\in V_2\}$. Which interval do you get?
Each subset of $\mathbb{R}^2$ below is cut out by two conditions on $\boldsymbol{x}=(x_1,x_2)$. Which of these subsets is convex?

In $\mathbb{R}^2$, let $V$ be the closed disc with centre $(1,0)$ and radius $1$, and let $\boldsymbol{p}=(0,2)$. Which set is $\{\boldsymbol{p}\}-V=\{\boldsymbol{p}-\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{x}\in V\}$?
options: The closed disc with centre $(1,2)$ and radius $1$
The closed disc with centre $(-1,2)$ and radius $1$
The closed disc with centre $(1,-2)$ and radius $1$
The closed disc with centre $(-1,2)$ and radius $2$

questions.question: Let $V_1,V_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty convex sets and $V_1-V_2=\{\boldsymbol{x}_1-\boldsymbol{x}_2\colon\boldsymbol{x}_1\in V_1,\ \boldsymbol{x}_2\in V_2\}$. Which statement about the zero vector and $V_1-V_2$ is correct?
options: $\boldsymbol{0}\in V_1-V_2$ if and only if $V_1\subseteq V_2$.
$\boldsymbol{0}\in V_1-V_2$ if and only if $V_1\cap V_2\neq\varnothing$.

questions.question: Let $V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty, $V+V=\{\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{y}\colon\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}\in V\}$ and $2V=\{2\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{x}\in V\}$. Which statement comparing $V+V$ and $2V$ is correct?
options: Always $2V\subseteq V+V$, with equality when $V$ is convex.
Always $V+V\subseteq2V$, with equality when $V$ is convex.
For convex $V$, $V+V=V$, since midpoints of $V$ stay in $V$.

questions.question: Let $U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$ be an open convex set and $F\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$ a closed convex set with $U\cap F\neq\varnothing$. What is guaranteed about $U\cap F$?
options: It is convex and closed, since intersections of closed sets are closed.
It is convex and open, since $U$ is open and $F$ only cuts it.
It is convex, but it can be neither open nor closed.
It need not be convex unless $U$ and $F$ are both open or both closed.

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}^2$, $V_1$ is the closed unit disc with centre $(0,0)$ and $V_2$ the closed unit disc with centre $(2,0)$; they touch at $(1,0)$. For which pair $\boldsymbol{p}\in V_1$, $\boldsymbol{q}\in V_2$ does the midpoint of $\boldsymbol{p}$ and $\boldsymbol{q}$ lie outside $V_1\cup V_2$?
In $\mathbb{R}^2$, let $V_1=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon x_1^2+x_2^2\le1\}$ and $V_2=\{(t,0)\colon 0\le t\le2\}$. Which point lies in $V_1+V_2$?
For each angle $\theta\in[0,2\pi)$, let $H_\theta=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1\cos\theta+x_2\sin\theta\le1\}$. Which set is the intersection $\bigcap_{\theta\in[0,2\pi)}H_\theta$?
Let $V_1$ and $V_2$ be nonempty convex sets in $\mathbb{R}^2$. Which statement about the union $V_1\cup V_2$ is correct?
options: If $V_1\cap V_2\neq\varnothing$, then $V_1\cup V_2$ is convex.
If $V_1\cup V_2$ is convex, then $V_1\subseteq V_2$ or $V_2\subseteq V_1$.
$V_1\cup V_2$ can be convex even when $V_1\cap V_2=\varnothing$.
If $V_1$ and $V_2$ are halfspaces, then $V_1\cup V_2$ is convex.

questions.question: Let $V_1,V_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty sets such that $V_1+V_2$ is convex. Which statement about the convexity of $V_1$ and $V_2$ is correct?
options: Both are convex, because $V_1=(V_1+V_2)-V_2$ is a difference of convex sets.
They need not be: in $\mathbb{R}$, $\{0,1\}+[0,1]=[0,2]$ is convex but $\{0,1\}$ is not.
$V_1$ is convex whenever $\boldsymbol{0}\in V_2$, since then $V_1\subseteq V_1+V_2$.
At least one of them is convex, since two nonconvex sets have a nonconvex sum.

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}^2$, let $V_1=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon x_1>0,\ x_1x_2\ge1\}$ and $V_2=\{(t,0)\colon t\in\mathbb{R}\}$; both sets are closed and convex. Which set is $V_1+V_2$?
In $\mathbb{R}^2$, let $V$ be the closed triangle with vertices $(0,0)$, $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$. Which set is $V-V=\{\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{y}\colon\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}\in V\}$?
